title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement:
An array of **distinct** integers was sorted in increasing order and then rotated at some unknown pivot: a prefix was cut off and moved to the end. For example `[3, 7, 9, 15, 18, 22]` might become `[15, 18, 22, 3, 7, 9]`. The rotation may also be zero, leaving the array fully sorted.

Given the rotated array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if it isn't there.

Your solution must run in **O(log n)** time.
constraints: all values in nums are distinct

target.note: O(log n) can't be told apart from O(n) at these sizes, so there's no benchmark — the requirement is checked by reading your code

hints: Split the array at any midpoint. Can both halves be unsorted, or is at least one of them always a normal sorted run?
At least one half is always sorted, and you can tell which by comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid]. For a sorted half, a range check tells you whether the target can be inside it.

Standard binary search on lo..hi. If nums[mid] is the target, return mid. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted: go left when nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], otherwise go right. Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right when nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], otherwise go left.
followups: How would you find the rotation point (the index of the minimum) in O(log n)?
What breaks if the array may contain duplicates, and what's the worst-case time then?
Could you solve it by finding the pivot first and then running an ordinary binary search? Compare the two approaches.
explain: Run binary search, but at each step decide which half is guaranteed sorted. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the run lo..mid has no rotation break, so the target is in it exactly when nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]; otherwise mid..hi is sorted and the target is in it exactly when nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]. Keep the half that could contain the target and discard the other. Each step halves the range: O(log n) time, O(1) space. Use <= in nums[lo] <= nums[mid] so the case lo == mid (two elements left) is treated as sorted. Compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 so lo + hi can't overflow.
